question.value: Characterize the dust continuum emission, spectral index, and dust emissivity index across disk and envelope scales (10 to 10^3 au) in the class 0/I YSO L1527 IRS to test for variations in dust properties and early grain growth.

evidence.quote: We aim to study the dust continuum emission of L1527 using the Atacama Large millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) to probe the outer ($10^3$ au) and inner ($10^2$ au) envelope, as well as the disk (10 au).
We aim to characterize the maximum grain size of the dust distribution in the envelope of a class 0/I YSO: L1527 IRS, or L1527 for short.

analysis_steps.goal: Model visibilities to disentangle compact disk and extended envelope emission

method.value: Fit a 10-parameter composite geometrical model (Gaussian for the compact disk plus a Plummer-like broken power law for the envelope) to the visibilities at each of the 5 frequencies using galario.

evidence.quote: Thus, we consider a geometrical model in which a Gaussian, that will trace the compact emission, is summed to a power law (Plummer profile)

In our framework, `galario` would compute a model image given our total profile, then it would Fourier-transform it into synthetic visibilities and sample them at the uv-points covered by the antenna configurations with which the observations were performed.

key_parameters.value: 10 free parameters: I_0 (f_0), r, sigma, inc, PA, R_in, R_out, p, dRA, dDec

evidence.quote: The 10 fit parameters were the flux amplitude $I_0$ and the $r$ factor; the width $\sigma$, the inclination (inc) and position angle (PA) of the Gaussian; the inner and outer envelope radii, $R_{in}$ and $R_{out}$, and the power law exponent $p$. Finally two parameters, dRA and dDec, fit the offset of the peak from the phase center.

assumptions.value: Envelope emission is constant within R_i, follows Plummer power law between R_i and R_out, and is zero beyond R_out; compact disk is represented by a 2D Gaussian

evidence.quote: These are such that the envelope emission is constant within a radius $R_i$, it follows Eq. [\[eq:total_profile\]](#eq:total_profile) between $R_i$ and $R_{out}$ and it is null beyond $R_{out}$.

fitting.value: Minimum-chi^2 MCMC fit using 80 walkers, 3,000 burn-in steps, and 7,000 post-burn-in steps (Figures 18-20 captions also note 50 or 60 walkers and 2000/5000 steps for some bands)

evidence.quote: Then, it would run a minimum-$\chi^2$ fit between the data and the model visibilities.
For each fit, 80 walkers were set to run for 3,000 burn-in steps and 7,000 more steps after the burn-in stage.

validation.value: Compared derived disk radius (~75 au in B7), inclination (~80 deg), and Plummer power-law exponent (p = 2.6-3.1) with literature values (Aso et al. 2017, Ladd et al. 1991); checked dRA and dDec are near zero

evidence.quote: If we define the radius of the disk to be the $2\sigma$ contour of the Gaussian component, then $R_{disk} \sim 75$ au in B7, consistent with what was found in the kinematical analysis of (cite: Aso2017).
Finally, the power law exponent of the Plummer profile ($p$) is found to be in the range 2.6-3.1, roughly consistent with what was found by (cite: Ladd1991).

analysis_steps.goal: Derive the envelope spectral index as a function of spatial scale and position angle

method.value: Subtract the best-fit galario Gaussian disk component from the visibilities, log-uniformly bin the residual envelope visibilities across uv-distance (starting from ~9 klambda), and perform a weighted linear regression to log10(F) vs log10(nu) across all 5 frequencies in each uv-bin, as well as in three position angle sectors (envelope, outflow, cavity walls) and between adjacent band pairs.

evidence.quote: Starting from the common shortest baseline of $\sim$ 9 k$\lambda$, we log-uniformly bin the visibilities across the available uv-distances and then measure the spectral index in each bin.
Since we are interested in studying the spectral index of the envelope, we have subtracted the galario best-fit Gaussian component of our model (see Section 3) from the data.
To make the best use of our multiwavelength data, we fitted a line to the fluxes along all wavelengths in each uv-distance bin and we more robustly determined the spectral index.

analysis_steps.goal: Compute temperature-corrected dust emissivity index beta(R) and fit its radial gradient

method.value: Check optical depth by comparing specific intensity F_0.88mm/Omega to Planck function B(T_dust) using a centrally illuminated envelope temperature profile; correct for departures from the Rayleigh-Jeans approximation by fitting log10[F_nu / B_nu(T)] = beta * log10(nu) + A in each uv-bin; fit a linear relation between beta and log10(R_au) using Bayesian linear regression in linmix.

evidence.quote: We find that, even at the shortest of our wavelengths, the envelope emission is optically thin at all scales as $F_{0.88mm}/\Omega < B(T_{dust})$ by a factor of 10 (Fig. 8).
We have run the fit by means of the Bayesian method described in (cite: Kelly2007) and implemented in linmix. The priors were uniformly distributed.

key_parameters.value: Radial scale range fitted: 50 to 2000 au

evidence.quote: We find evidence for an outward increasing $\beta$, rising from 0.8 to 1.6 between 50 and 2000 au radial scales

assumptions.value: Dust temperature profile T(R) = 38 L^0.2 (R / 100 au)^-0.4 with L_bol = 1.6 L_sun and d = 140 pc

evidence.quote: To evaluate the optical thickness, we consider a typical dust temperature prescription for a centrally illuminated protostellar envelope ((cite: Shu1977), (cite: Butner1990), (cite: Terebey1993), (cite: Motte2001)): $$\begin{equation} T(R) = 38 L^{0.2} \Bigg(\frac{R}{100 au}\Bigg)^{-0.4}. \label{eq:temp} \end{equation}$$

assumptions.value: Envelope continuum emission is optically thin at all studied wavelengths and scales, and temperature profile is exact so Delta_beta = Delta_alpha

evidence.quote: The error on the dust emissivity index has been considered to be the same one that affects the spectral index since we are assuming an exact temperature profile, thus $\Delta\alpha = \Delta\beta$.

claims.hypothesis: Dust properties vary across the envelope of the class 0/I protostar L1527 IRS, with larger grains present in the inner envelope.
claims.experiment: Combined archival and new FAUST ALMA/ACA continuum visibilities across Bands 3, 4, 6, and 7 (5 frequencies), subtracted a 2D Gaussian disk model fitted with galario, and derived the temperature-corrected dust emissivity index beta(R) from 50 to 2000 au.
claims.result: Found a tentative outward gradient beta(R_au) = 0.37(+0.17/-0.16) log10(R_au) - 0.23(+0.45/-0.46), rising from 0.8 at 50 au to 1.6 at 2000 au, with beta <= 1 below ~300 au.
claims.finding: There is tentative evidence for variations in dust optical properties in the L1527 envelope, consistent with ISM-like grains at 2000 au and submillimeter-sized grains below 300 au.

evidence.quote: We find evidence for an outward increasing $\beta$, rising from 0.8 to 1.6 between 50 and 2000 au radial scales

These measurements represent tentative evidence for dust optical properties variations throughout the envelope of L1527. Furthermore, low $\beta$ at scales lower than $\sim$ 300 au are consistent with the presence of submillimeter sized grains in the inner envelope.

claims.hypothesis: The circumstellar disk of L1527 IRS can have its grain sizes constrained from its millimeter spectral energy distribution.
claims.experiment: Extracted the compact disk flux across five ALMA frequencies (0.86 to 3.4 mm) via uv-plane Gaussian+Plummer modeling and combined them with VLA measurements up to 6 cm to fit the disk SED.
claims.result: Measured a disk spectral index alpha = 2.1 +/- 0.1 between 0.88 and 7 mm and a free-free slope alpha_35-60 = 0.33 +/- 0.17.
claims.finding: The edge-on circumstellar disk is optically thick at millimeter wavelengths, preventing any constraint on disk dust grain properties from the spectral index alone.

evidence.quote: Fitting the SED in the 0.88 to 7-millimeter range using our measurements along with the values of (cite: Melis2011), we find an optically thick disk with $\alpha = 2.1 \pm 0.1$.
The high optical depth of the circumstellar disk of L1527 prevents us from concluding anything about its dust grain properties based on the spectral index alone.

claims.hypothesis: Protostellar outflows or cavity walls in L1527 exhibit a different dust spectral index from the infalling envelope at large scales.
claims.experiment: Divided the disk-subtracted uv-plane visibilities into three position angle sectors corresponding to the envelope (-20 to 20 deg), outflow (70 to 110 deg), and cavity walls, and measured the spectral index in each sector.
claims.result: The spectral index profiles in the three angular sectors show no significant differences at scales larger than 200 au.
claims.finding: There is no significant azimuthal variation in the spectral index between the envelope, outflow, and cavity walls beyond 200 au.

evidence.quote: We divided the uv-plane into three different regions: the envelope ($-20^\circ< PA <20^\circ$), the outflow ($70^\circ< PA <110^\circ$) and the cavity walls (the remaining zones). We do not observe any significant difference among the three spectral indices at scales larger than 200 au (Fig. 7).

claims.hypothesis: Multifrequency (n > 2), multiscale high-sensitivity observations substantially improve constraints on the spectral and dust emissivity indices of faint protostellar envelopes compared to two-wavelength studies.
claims.experiment: Compared the 5-frequency weighted linear regression across ALMA Bands 3, 4, 6, and 7 over 9.8-1000 klambda with two-band adjacent spectral indices and with previous two-frequency PdBI measurements (Galametz et al. 2019).
claims.result: Adjacent band pairs show large uncertainties at long baselines and systematic offsets, whereas combining all four ALMA bands halves the error bars on beta compared to the two-wavelength PdBI study (sigma_beta = 0.08 vs 0.16) and doubles the spatial dynamic range.
claims.finding: A multiscale, multifrequency (n > 2), high-sensitivity approach is necessary to damp two-band systematics and halve the uncertainties on envelope spectral and dust emissivity indices.

evidence.quote: We argue that a multiscale ($10^1-10^3$ au), multifrequency (n>2), and high-sensitivity study is necessary to tightly constrain the spectral- and dust emissivity index profiles of faint class 0/I YSO envelopes.
Using ALMA B3, B4, B6 and B7 effectively halves the error bars of measurements made in previous studies that made use of two wavelengths only.

why_this_data.value: L1527 is nearby (140 pc), bright, and extensively observed across four ALMA bands (B3, B4, B6, B7) with both the 12m and 7m arrays, allowing a deep continuum combination covering 9.8 to 1000 klambda to simultaneously resolve the compact disk and recover the faint extended envelope.

evidence.quote: Due to its distance and brightness, L1527 is one of the best studied class 0/I YSOs.
We collect every available ALMA and ACA dataset suitable for our study of L1527, aiming to combine them in the deepest continuum analysis of the envelope so far.

evidence.loc: L1527 as seen in the visibility space
evidence.quote: On top of enriching the studied frequency range, we used a combination of ALMA and ACA data to study the dust continuum emission with high S/N at scales 2 times larger than G19, toward both shorter and longer baselines.

why_this_method.value: Working directly in the uv-plane avoids image reconstruction artifacts and non-linearities, and fitting a composite Gaussian + Plummer model across 9.8-1000 klambda removes the resolved disk more accurately than subtracting a constant long-baseline amplitude.

evidence.loc: L1527 as seen in the visibility space
evidence.quote: Considering the wider uv-coverage of the data we used (9.8-1000 k$\lambda$), we can more precisely model and subtract the compact emission by fitting a Gaussian component within a model that separately accounts for envelope and disk (see Section 3).

To investigate dust properties in the envelope of L1527, we worked in the visibility ($u, v$) plane. This approach has the main advantage of keeping the analysis clear of the artifacts and non-linearity from which image reconstruction algorithms suffer.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Subtracting a constant visibility amplitude (F_200klambda) to remove the disk, as done in Galametz et al. (2019) and Miotello et al. (2014), was rejected in favor of fitting a 2D Gaussian + Plummer profile because the disk is resolved at long baselines.

evidence.loc: L1527 as seen in the visibility space
evidence.quote: G19 subtracted a constant amplitude (F$_{200 k\lambda}$) from each visibility at the two frequencies, assuming an unresolved disk that would contribute a constant flux at baselines shorter than 200 k$\lambda$ ($\sim$1.0$''$, or 140 au).

evidence.loc: L1527 as seen in the visibility space
evidence.quote: Considering the wider uv-coverage of the data we used (9.8-1000 k$\lambda$), we can more precisely model and subtract the compact emission by fitting a Gaussian component within a model that separately accounts for envelope and disk (see Section 3).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Computing spectral indices from only two adjacent frequency bands was shown to suffer from large uncertainties and systematic differences compared to fitting all five frequencies simultaneously.

evidence.quote: Moreover, the spectral index $\alpha$ shows systematic differences among different combination of adjacent bands. Only using multiple bands (>2), one can robustly constrain the spectral index, damping the uncertainties that arise using only two frequencies (see Section 4).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Explaining low inner-envelope beta (<1) solely via dust composition/porosity variations or a much colder envelope temperature (<5 K at 300 au) was rejected as physically unreasonable.

evidence.loc: Grain size, composition and temperature effects on $\beta$
evidence.quote: However, to produce $\beta \sim$ 1.7, the temperature of the envelope at 300 au would need to be lower than 5 K, which is far below a reasonable value for a protostellar envelope.
None of these possibilities alone are able to justify $\beta$ values as low as 1 at hundreds of au, thus strengthening the hypothesis of submillimeter grains at these scales.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: In situ coagulation of millimeter grains in the low-density envelope is disfavored by theoretical models, so differential collapse of prestellar core grains or outflow transport of grown disk grains are considered as viable alternatives.

evidence.quote: While in situ formation seems disfavored by most theoretical studies, differential core dust collapse or outflow dust transport from the disk could explain our observations.

how_they_decided_enough.value: Collected almost every available archival ALMA/ACA dataset to maximize S/N; stopped self-calibration at 10s intervals when shorter intervals gave no further S/N improvement; tested temperature profile exponents from -0.3 to -0.6 to verify robustness of beta.

evidence.quote: We did not find any appreciable improvement in the noise and signal-to-noise properties for phase-only self-calibration steps with even smaller time intervals.
We also investigated the effects on $\beta$ of changing the temperature profile’s radial power law exponent. We found that exponents in the interval [-0.3,-0.6] do not affect our conclusions.

limitations_admitted.value: A given interferometric baseline B probes all structures within scale theta ~ lambda/B rather than an isolated annulus, so the derived alpha and beta at a given uv-distance represent flux-weighted averages that can be dominated by the brighter inner envelope.

evidence.quote: First, while we present a study of the spectral- and dust emissivity indices as a function of uv-distance and physical source scales, we have to keep in mind that a particular baseline does not only probe an annular region at some distance from the center, rather it probes any physical structure within a scale given by $\theta \sim \lambda/B$.
If the inner envelope is much brighter than the outer one, as expected, the flux at even the shorter baselines will be dominated by the inner envelope.

limitations_admitted.value: The dust emissivity index derivation relies on a simple 1D analytical power-law temperature profile T proportional to R^-0.4 rather than 3D radiative transfer modeling with temperature uncertainties.

evidence.quote: a more thorough treatment that accounts for the temperature structure and its associated uncertainties can be achieved by post-processing 3D envelope models with radiative transfer in order to.

limitations_admitted.value: High optical depth of the edge-on disk prevents extracting dust grain properties within the disk without radiative transfer modeling.

evidence.quote: No dust grain properties information can be extracted in such a condition without thorough radiative transfer modelling, outside of the scope of this work.

referee_caveats_inferred: Deprojecting and mapping uv-distance directly to a physical radius R_au (via R ~ lambda/B) treats the visibility amplitude at baseline B as local to radius R, whereas the Fourier transform of a power-law envelope mixes emission across scales.

The Gaussian + Plummer visibility fit is performed independently in each frequency band, resulting in band-dependent envelope outer radii (R_out = 1.35'' in B7 vs 12.8'' in B4) and disk widths (sigma = 0.147'' to 0.330''), so subtracting the fitted Gaussian removes slightly different spatial structures at each frequency.

Primary beam attenuation at large scales (19'' FWHM in B7 for the 12m array) is estimated to be ~10% at 20 klambda, but visibilities from 12m and 7m arrays are concatenated directly in the uv-plane without joint primary-beam deconvolution.
